insider_note: Over a symmetric range the factor of π/2 appears only when BOTH powers are even. Here the cosine power is 7, which is odd, so no π/2 survives — unlike sin²θcos⁴θ, where it does.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Show the integrand is an even function
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos(−θ)=cosθ always, regardless of the power — only sin's own oddness matters, and here it is squared away.
steps.memory_tip: cosθ is itself an even function, so cosⁿθ is always even in θ, whatever n is.

lines.text: whether the integrand is even or odd.

steps.why: Squaring sin(−θ)=−sinθ removes the sign, and raising cos(−θ)=cosθ to the odd power 7 keeps it positive since cos itself is already unchanged under θ→−θ, so the product is unchanged overall.
common_mistakes: Assuming an odd power of cosine makes the whole function odd — it is cos(−θ)=cosθ itself that matters, not the parity of the exponent.
Skipping the parity check and integrating directly over the full symmetric range.

steps.label: Double the half-range integral and evaluate
steps.margin_note: Second mark. K=1 here because n=7 is odd, even though m=2 is even — BOTH powers must be even for the π/2 factor.
steps.memory_tip: One odd power among the two is enough to keep K=1 — only two even powers together bring in π/2.

lines.text: Wallis's formula, m = 2, n = 7 (odd), so K = 1:

steps.why: Doubling the half-range integral and applying Wallis's mixed-power formula (m=2 even, n=7 odd, so K=1) gives 2×16/315=32/315.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to double after establishing the function is even.
Including a π/2 factor even though n=7 is odd, which forces K=1.
